units.title: Behavioral specifications, policy boundaries and threat models
outcomes: Separate intended behavior, observed compliance and unresolved policy choices.
Map an LLM application's assets, actors, access, trust boundaries and residual consequences to testable claims.
Specify expected behavior for benign, ambiguous and disallowed requests before labeling outputs.
units.why: Build on Security goals, trust boundaries and threat models. Here the new job is to connect a model behavior to a plausible harm and a measurable policy boundary, not just draw the system.

next.note: Measure both sides of the policy boundary.

study.title: OpenAI Model Spec, 2026-08-18: one worked behavior contract
study.locator: Instructions and levels of authority; The chain of command, especially Follow all applicable instructions and Ignore untrusted data by default; Protect people's privacy
study.depth: Read these sections and their examples only. Treat the vendor's choices as an example, not a universal policy or evidence of compliance.

study.title: ARENA 3.1: Threat-Modeling & Specification Design
study.locator: What are evals trying to achieve?; Threat-Modeling; Specification; Question Design
study.depth: Work by hand. Skip hosted API calls and the alignment-faking replication.

study.title: NIST AI 600-1: policy and threat-model ownership
study.locator: Section 3, GOVERN 3.2: GV-3.2-003 (acceptable use and refusal criteria) and GV-3.2-005 (threat modeling)

focus: Write the deployment scope first: a local assistant with offline documents and no real credentials or external actions. Name who can edit user messages, retrieved text and tool results.
Give every test a policy clause, expected behavior, severity and rationale. Clarification and safe assistance are distinct from refusal.
Connect each threat to an asset, attacker capability, entry point, mitigation, detection signal and residual consequence. Record assumptions the experiment cannot test.
Freeze the specification before labels. Keep disputed normative cases visible rather than relabeling them to match a benchmark.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, trace a fake instruction in a retrieved document through an offline assistant to an unauthorized disclosure of a synthetic secret. Mark the authority boundary, then write one benign request, one ambiguous request and one disallowed request with expected behavior and the policy clause that decides each.
traps: Calling a specification an empirical safety result. It states what should happen; the campaign measures what actually happens.
Treating a model's stated intentions or multiple-choice answer as proof of its motives. Measure behavior under a stated protocol instead.
Letting the benchmark silently define policy. Its labels may disagree with your intended application.

selfTest.q: A retrieved page says it is a system message. Does that grant it authority?
selfTest.a: No. Its provenance remains untrusted retrieved data. A textual claim of authority does not change the message's trust boundary.

selfTest.q: Why keep ambiguous requests in the specification?
selfTest.a: They test clarification and context-sensitive assistance. A binary refuse-or-comply policy can hide both unsafe completions and unnecessary refusals.

selfTest.q: A test passes, but its assumed tool permission is absent in the application. What follows?
selfTest.a: The result describes that test configuration, not the proposed harm pathway. Reconcile the access assumption before using it in the safety argument.

practice.name: ARENA 3.1: Build threat models; Design a specification
practice.locator: Exercises Build threat models and Design a specification
practice.note: Adapt one property to your offline assistant. Write the causal scenario and operational definitions by hand; no paid API is needed. Keep the assumptions and unresolved choices for the campaign.

units.stopWhen: Your written scope and policy decide the three boundary cases, and every modeled threat ends in a testable claim or an owned evidence gap.

fit.note: The dated Model Spec, ARENA design exercises and NIST actions cover the policy, threat and ownership job without a new resource.

units.title: Harmful capability versus harmful compliance, refusal and overrefusal
outcomes: Measure harmful compliance, refusal and benign overrefusal as separate outcomes.
Distinguish failed elicitation from evidence that a model lacks a capability.
Diagnose a safety-score gain caused by indiscriminate refusal or degraded answer quality.
units.why: A model can stop saying refusal phrases without producing useful harmful content. It can also improve a safety score by refusing everything. This unit establishes the two-sided baseline for the campaign.

next.note: Check whether the instrument can distinguish these outcomes.

study.title: CS336 Spring 2026 Assignment 5 supplement, Version 26.0.0
study.locator: Sections 3.4 and 5.4: SimpleSafetyTests before and after SFT, problems `sst_baseline` and `sst_sft`
study.depth: Keep the before/after protocol, not the large models or hosted setup. Use the small-model substitute in Practice and hand labels instead of the 70B grader.

study.title: XSTest: safe and unsafe contrast prompts
StrongREJECT, arXiv:2402.10260v1
study.locator: Section 2.2, Response evaluation; Section 3.4, Our StrongREJECT autograder; Sections 6.2 and 6.3 on capability degradation
study.depth: Study the rubric and controls. Do not run its paid or gated graders.

focus: The pinned XSTest table has 250 safe prompts and 200 unsafe contrast prompts. Preserve row IDs and report denominators separately; a small subset is not the full benchmark.
Label refusal, policy violation and useful assistance separately. A disclaimer followed by a disallowed answer remains a violation; a harmless off-topic answer is not useful compliance.
Use the written policy to adjudicate borderline cases. Review offensive or distressing examples privately and stop review when needed; do not publish raw harmful generations.
Freeze checkpoint, template, decoding, token budget and item IDs across comparisons. Failed generations remain in the ledger with explicit status.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, construct a score table for an always-refuse assistant and an always-answer assistant on your policy-labeled safe and unsafe slices. The first has complete overrefusal on safe requests and no harmful compliance if its refusals contain no disallowed content. The second's harmful-compliance rate still depends on what its answers actually contain, not just the absence of refusal words.
traps: Calling non-refusal an attack success. StrongREJECT checks whether the answer actually addresses the harmful goal.
Calling failure on one prompt proof of absent capability. Prompting, output budget and model comprehension can all limit elicitation.
Using XSTest's string labels as policy truth. Its prefix matcher has no partial-compliance category and can mistake an apology for a full refusal.

selfTest.q: Can refusal rate rise while useful safety gets worse?
selfTest.a: Yes. Benign requests may be refused more often while harmful completions persist. Inspect both slices and the content of each answer.

selfTest.q: An encoded attack produces nonsense rather than a refusal. Is it successful?
selfTest.a: Not on that evidence. Non-refusal alone does not establish useful harmful assistance; the encoding may have destroyed comprehension.

selfTest.q: Why not pool the safe and unsafe denominators?
selfTest.a: Their desired behaviors differ. A pooled score changes with the slice mixture and can hide benign utility loss.

practice.name: CS336 supplement: `sst_baseline` and `sst_sft`, reduced-scale adaptation
practice.locator: Sections 3.4 and 5.4; retain prompts, raw generations and item-level scores
practice.note: Use your existing small SFT checkpoint and its parent. Otherwise use HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct at revision 12fd25f77366fa6b3b4b768ec3050bf629380bac as a single baseline, with transformers 5.19 and PyTorch 2.14.1. Generate a preselected small harm-area-balanced SimpleSafetyTests subset and a type-balanced XSTest subset on your GPU or CPU, one request at a time. Record the chat template and a fixed short output budget. Hand-score both; there are no public safety-label tests. Do not claim an SFT effect without two related checkpoints. The handouts and tests are public study material; never publish course solutions.

units.stopWhen: Your baseline report separates harmful compliance, safe-prompt overrefusal and useful benign answers, with item IDs, raw outputs, failure counts and a stated elicitation limit.

fit.note: The CS336 experiment, pinned XSTest and StrongREJECT rubric jointly cover compliance, overrefusal and capability confounds at small scale.

units.title: Jailbreak, prompt-injection and multi-turn attacks, and adaptive red teaming
outcomes: Implement a bounded adaptive attack loop with complete query and feedback provenance.
Distinguish direct jailbreaks, indirect injection and target-side multi-turn attacks.
Measure mitigation generalization on attack families excluded from development.
units.why: Build on Tenant isolation, input validation and injection. LLM attacks add natural-language instruction conflicts and adaptive feedback, so a fixed prompt list cannot establish resistance to a changing attacker.

next.note: Retest defenses against an attacker allowed to adapt.

study.title: Indirect prompt injection, arXiv:2302.12173v1
study.locator: Figures 1 and 2; Section 3, Attack Surface of Application-Integrated Large Language Models; Section 4, Discussion
study.depth: Read the trust boundaries and synthetic application, not the product demonstrations as current vulnerabilities. Never target a live third-party system.

study.title: PAIR, arXiv:2310.08419v1
study.locator: Section 3, especially Algorithm 1 and Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4
study.depth: Reconstruct one serial stream. Skip published multi-model sweeps and hosted attackers or judges.

study.title: CS336 supplement: red-team after instruction tuning

focus: A direct jailbreak tries to override policy through the user's request. Indirect injection arrives through lower-trust retrieved content. Multi-turn attacks preserve target conversation state; record it explicitly.
PAIR retains attacker history but normally gives the target a fresh candidate prompt. Do not describe that alone as target-side multi-turn evaluation.
Retain parent attack ID, source, family, edits, feedback, target checkpoint, full transcript, query count and token budget. Count unsuccessful and malformed attempts too.
Split by attack family and source before tuning. Freeze the defense, then allow a fresh, budget-matched adaptation on held-out families without changing the defense again.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw one PAIR stream from candidate to target response to judged feedback to revised candidate. Then contrast it with a target conversation that retains earlier turns. Give each an explicit stopping budget and show which transcript must be restored to replay an unsuccessful attempt.
traps: Reporting only the winning prompt. Selection consumed failed queries and can overstate a method's efficiency.
Counting paraphrases of a training attack as held-out families. Shared templates and sources can leak across the split.
Using a fake secret copied into the attack itself as extraction evidence. Success must require crossing the boundary, not echoing attacker-supplied text.

selfTest.q: Two attacks each succeed once, but one uses more retries. Are their success rates comparable?
selfTest.a: Not without a common budget and success unit. Report success per behavior under the same query and token limits, plus the cost of all attempts.

selfTest.q: Does an attacker editing a retrieved document need control of the user's prompt?
selfTest.a: No. Retrieval can carry attacker text into the assistant even when the user makes an ordinary request.

selfTest.q: Why rerun an adaptive attacker after installing a defense?
selfTest.a: A defense may only block known strings. Fresh feedback tests whether the attacker can route around it within the declared budget.

practice.name: CS336 supplement: `red_teaming`, local adaptive extension
practice.note: Use the frozen small checkpoint and software from Harmful capability versus harmful compliance, refusal and overrefusal. Bound one stream to five target queries per behavior; act as the attacker by hand and hand-check feedback. Include direct, offline retrieved-text and target-history cases using invented policy violations only. Disable network tools and real credentials. This is a reduced manual adaptation, not a PAIR replication. Keep regression fixtures for the query cap and transcript replay; the course has no public attack-success tests. Never publish course solutions.

units.stopWhen: You can replay every attempt, enforce the declared budget, and report static versus adaptive outcomes on a family-held-out slice with all failures retained.

fit.note: The injection paper supplies trust boundaries, PAIR supplies the feedback loop, and the named CS336 exercise anchors bounded local practice.

units.title: Memorization, training-data extraction and sensitive-information leakage
outcomes: Measure extraction of planted synthetic canaries under a declared access and query budget.
Separate training-data memorization, prefix-assisted discovery and leakage from the current context.
Explain why a failed extraction attempt and low perplexity alone cannot establish a privacy guarantee.
units.why: Build on Membership inference, extraction, inversion and poisoning and Contamination and memorization. The new evidence is controlled exposure in your own training pipeline, not searching a pretrained model for real people's records.

next.note: Carry exposure limits and untested privacy risks into the release decision.

study.title: Carlini et al., USENIX Security 2021 proceedings
study.locator: Section 3, Training Data Extraction, especially Definitions 1 and 2, Section 3.2 threat model and Section 3.4 ethics; Section 5.2, Improved Membership Inference
study.depth: Study the generation-and-ranking method, but replace all real-data discovery and validation with your own invented canaries. Do not reproduce Internet searches for personal records.

study.title: Nasr et al., arXiv:2311.17035v1
study.locator: Section 1, Ethics & Responsible Disclosure; Section 3.1, Prior Approaches and Definitions; Section 3.5, Discoverable Mem. vs. Extractable Mem.
study.depth: Stop at the definitions and limits. Production-endpoint attacks and large-corpus searches are not practice.

focus: Plant invented random strings in a known number of training documents. Track document multiplicity separately from repeated occurrences and actual token exposure.
Use an untouched checkpoint and untrained canaries as controls. Keep all secret suffixes out of prompts, retrieval, judge instructions and logs exposed to the target.
Predeclare byte-exact suffix matching, prefix lengths, decoding and total attempts. Report prefix-assisted and unprompted results separately, including negative results.
Perplexity or a reference-model ratio ranks candidates; it does not prove membership. Matching a known planted suffix supplies ground truth for this experiment only.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, design a canary experiment with a training-exposed string, an untrained control string and an unchanged checkpoint. Specify which prefix the attacker knows and which suffix must be generated. Draw a separate path for a synthetic secret present only in retrieved context, and explain why that path tests context leakage rather than training memorization.
traps: Scoring tokens supplied in the prefix as extracted content. Score only the withheld suffix and record how much context the attack received.
Interpreting non-extraction as non-memorization. A finite attack can miss stored information or lack a suitable prompt.
Assuming public information has no privacy risk. Reproduction in a new context can violate contextual integrity.

selfTest.q: A canary occurs ten times in one training document. Is its document multiplicity ten?
selfTest.a: No. It is one document under the paper's definition. Repeated occurrences and token exposure are separate experimental quantities.

selfTest.q: A low-perplexity completion looks like an address. Does it prove extraction?
selfTest.a: No. It may be common, fabricated or inferable. This exercise verifies only exact matches to known synthetic training records.

selfTest.q: Why compare with an unchanged checkpoint?
selfTest.a: It helps distinguish an effect of your planted-data training from pre-existing completion behavior. It does not by itself prove that every observed difference is memorization.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a bounded synthetic-canary exposure study on your existing tiny decoder, with an unchanged checkpoint, untrained canaries, withheld suffixes, complete query records and a separate synthetic context-leakage test. Reuse the recorded training stack; CPU with a smaller decoder is sufficient. No real personal data or production endpoint is involved.
units.stopWhen: Your privacy evidence distinguishes exposure from discovery, includes controls and failed queries, and states exactly which matching rule and attack budget the result supports.

fit.note: Carlini supplies the threat and ranking method; Nasr supplies the discoverability distinction. The campaign supplies controlled synthetic-only practice.
